issues.legal_issue: A category-based exemption from rent regulation for buildings belonging to public religious or charitable institutions is not an impermissible classification when it serves the institutions’ public purposes.
material_facts: The government issued notifications exempting buildings owned by religious institutions and related bodies from several provisions regulating leases, rent, and eviction.
The exempted owners were religious or charitable institutions whose income and its use were governed by their institutional objects.
The exemption was intended to allow those institutions to carry out their purposes.
The challenge relied on the fact that the exemption covered a broad category of buildings, including buildings used commercially.
issues.conclusion: The category is distinct from private landlords, and exempting its buildings was not arbitrary or contrary to Article 14; the notifications were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 25 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, the government may grant an exemption in the public interest or for other sufficient cause, but may not exercise that power arbitrarily. Article 14 prohibits arbitrary discrimination. In P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, religious and charitable trusts were treated as a distinct class; S. Kandaswamy Chettiar v. State of Tamil Nadu upheld a total exemption for public religious or charitable trusts because they serve public purposes and their income is governed by their objects. The Court also relied on Jayakaran v. Kerala Health R&W Society, State of Kerala v. Vijayan, and Lakshmanan v. Mohamood in rejecting distinctions based on ownership or the breadth of the exempted category.

predicates.rent_exemption_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges government notifications that exempt a category of buildings from rent regulation.
predicates.public_religious_charitable_owners: The buildings belong to public religious or charitable institutions whose income and its use are governed by their institutional objects.
predicates.exemption_serves_institutional_objects: The government granted the exemption to enable the institutions to carry out their public religious or charitable purposes.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a category-based rent exemption for buildings of public religious or charitable institutions, and the exemption serves their institutional objects, the category exemption is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge alleging non-application of mind is not made out merely because an exemption notification gives no specific reasons or the record lacks case-specific evidence of likely tenant exploitation, where the exemption rests on an established public-interest basis for the relevant institutional category.
material_facts: The notifications did not set out specific reasons for granting the exemptions.
The State supported the exemptions in its counter affidavit by relying on the law concerning religious and charitable institutions.
Earlier decisions had recognized such institutions as a distinct class and had upheld comparable exemptions, including exemptions granted in the State.
There was no material showing that the landlords in the cases would exploit tenants by charging market rent or evicting them for failure to pay it.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in finding that the government had not applied its mind; the absence of further case-specific material did not justify quashing the notifications, which were valid.
issues.legal_principle: The exercise of exemption power must be reasonable and based on a relevant public-interest or sufficient-cause basis. Under Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. S.D. Agarwal, a court may infer non-application of mind where there is no material on which the authority could form the required opinion. Here, the Court considered the recognized distinct status of religious and charitable institutions and earlier decisions applying that principle. It also relied on Jayakaran v. Kerala Health R&W Society for the proposition that reasons for an exemption need not appear in the notification if they are stated in the counter affidavit.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges rent-exemption notifications for public religious or charitable institutions, the notifications give no specific reasons, the government supports a public-interest basis, and comparable exemptions have previously been upheld, the non-application-of-mind challenge fails.
